clue.text: Pull old-fashioned woman over for being a slowcoach

indicators.note: turning something over flips it, so the joined words are read from the end back to the start

parts.note: to drag is to pull
gal is a dated word for a girl or woman

explanation.surface: Someone drags a dawdling, old-fashioned lady out of the way for holding everyone up.
explanation.definitionFit: A laggard is a person who falls behind or moves slowly, exactly what a slowcoach is.

clue.text: One-time great still not caught

parts.note: a means one
T is the abbreviation for time
large means great in size

explanation.surface: A former star remains on the run from the law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One-time' looks like 'former', but it splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A fugitive at large is free and has not yet been captured by the authorities.

clue.text: Party conference speaker betting the election ends in disaster

indicators.note: a disaster is chaos, so these letters fall into disorder
the ends of words are their final letters, one from each

parts.note: the final letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: A speaker at a party conference gambles that the vote will end badly.
explanation.definitionFit: The Green Party is a political party campaigning on environmental issues, often just called the Greens.

clue.text: Stealing jewellery worn by Bob, model

indicators.note: jewellery worn by someone goes around them, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: a ring is a piece of jewellery

indicators.note: to model is to shape, so these letters are reshaped into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A thief steals the jewels that a man named Bob, a model, is wearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Robbing means taking property unlawfully from someone, the same as stealing.

clue.text: Have gangs taken over society?

indicators.note: in an across clue one thing placed over another simply comes before it

parts.note: posses are bands of people, gangs
S is the standard abbreviation for society

explanation.surface: A worried question about whether gangsters have seized control of the community.
explanation.definitionFit: To possess something is to own or hold it, the same as having it.

clue.text: Fancy hotel ad: 'Not English or dated'

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or imagined, so these letters are freely rearranged
not means without, so that letter is removed

parts.note: taken as written
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A snooty hotel advertisement boasting it is neither English nor out of date.
explanation.definitionFit: Old hat is an idiom for something stale and out of fashion, matching dated.

clue.text: Looked over scrambled egg, amazed

indicators.note: one piece lies over the other on both sides, enclosing it

parts.note: stared means looked hard

indicators.note: scrambling mixes things up, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone gazes, astonished, at a plate of scrambled eggs.
explanation.definitionFit: To be staggered is to be astonished or shocked, so a synonym for amazed.

clue.text: Group available to be released

parts.note: a set is a group
free means available, not busy

explanation.surface: A band announces it is free to be let go.
explanation.definitionFit: Set free is a phrasal verb meaning liberated from captivity, the same as released.

clue.text: New road cannot be remade flat

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new

indicators.note: something remade is constructed again in a different form, so its letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A fresh road surface cannot be relaid level.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat' suggests a level road, but it describes a drink that has lost its fizz.
explanation.definitionFit: A non-carbonated drink has no bubbles, so it is still or flat like a lemonade gone stale.

clue.text: Colour at the heart of nebula that's exploding

indicators.note: something exploding is blown apart, so its letters land in a new order
the heart of a word is its inside, with the outer letters stripped away

parts.note: the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: An astronomer describes the colour glowing in the core of a bursting gas cloud.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue is one of the primary colours of the spectrum, a simple example of the category.

clue.text: Publicises actors moving into Norfolk area

indicators.note: the actors move inside the area, so one word sits within the other

parts.note: the Norfolk Broads are a region of lakes and rivers in eastern England
the cast is the body of actors in a production

explanation.surface: A tourist board advertises that a troupe of actors is relocating to the Norfolk countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: The Broads are a well-known network of shallow lakes and waterways in Norfolk, an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: To broadcast news is to spread it widely, so broadcasts is a verb form matching publicises.

clue.text: Metal device Apple might make for Reagan?

parts.note: Apple names its products with a lower-case i prefix: iPhone, iPad, iMac
Ronald Reagan, the US president, was known as Ron

explanation.surface: Wondering what gadget the tech company might design specially for a former US president.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is an Apple-style product named after Ronald Reagan, an i-Ron.
explanation.definitionFit: An iron is both a chemical element among the metals and a household appliance for pressing clothes, so a metal device.

clue.text: Labour leader's suppressing rage following Conservative mistakes

indicators.note: what follows comes after, so the built piece is placed after the next one

parts.note: C is the usual abbreviation for Conservative

indicators.note: to suppress something is to hold it down within, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: the first letter of Labour, with the possessive s kept
rage is a synonym of anger

explanation.surface: A political report: the Labour leader is holding back fury after a string of Tory blunders.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a clanger is an embarrassing blunder, as in dropping a clanger.
explanation.definitionFit: Clangers are glaring, embarrassing errors in British informal speech, so a plural synonym for mistakes.

clue.text: Young people take drugs into strange building

indicators.note: the drugs are taken into the other piece, so they sit inside it
building means constructing something new, so these letters are put together afresh

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
E stands for ecstasy, so two of them make drugs

explanation.surface: A warning that youngsters are bringing narcotics into an odd-looking building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' looks like an adjective describing the building, but it is the word to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Teenagers are adolescents aged thirteen to nineteen, a common example of youngsters.

clue.text: Owl, say, to peck enthusiast according to Spooner

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the initial sounds trade places

parts.note: to peck is to give a little bite; it takes the opening sound of the other word
a nerd is an obsessive enthusiast; it takes the opening sound of the other word

explanation.surface: An owl pecking at an eager fan, told in Spooner's style.
explanation.walkthrough: Spooner swaps the opening sounds of the two words, so the b and the n trade places.
explanation.definitionFit: A night bird is one active after dark, and the owl is the classic example.

clue.text: Supporters welcome end of power plants

indicators.note: to welcome someone is to take them in, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: golf tees hold up, or support, the ball

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter only

parts.note: the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Backers of some cause greet the collapse of power stations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plants' reads as power stations in the surface, but it is the botanical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Trees are large woody perennial growths, an example of plants in the botanical sense.

clue.text: Treatment of waste 50% removed for you and me

indicators.note: half of a word is taken out and something else put in its place

parts.note: sewage is waste matter carried in drains
us refers to you and me together

explanation.surface: A report on processing effluent, half of which has been cleared away for our benefit.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half of the six-letter word for waste, SEW, is swapped for US.
explanation.definitionFit: Usage is the way something is handled or used, as in rough usage, so a synonym for treatment.

clue.text: Before heading to UK, this criminal kidnaps husband with unknown dog

indicators.note: what comes before is placed earlier, so the built piece precedes the last one
a kidnapper holds a victim inside, so one piece goes within the other
something criminal is crooked, so these letters are bent out of order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
H is the abbreviation for husband
z is a mathematical unknown

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: Before flying home, a crook abducts a man and his mystery dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A shih tzu is a small long-haired toy breed originally from Tibet and China, an example of a dog.

clue.text: Playwright: I see Earnest initially getting cold feet

parts.note: Noel Coward was an English playwright
taken as written
the word is pronounced like the letter C

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A dramatist notices that The Importance of Being Earnest is losing its nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: Earnest evokes Wilde's play, but it supplies only its first letter; 'see' gives C because the two sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Cold feet is the idiom for losing courage before acting, which is a form of cowardice.

clue.text: Drink mixed in baths

indicators.note: mixing stirs things together, so these letters end up in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A cocktail stirred up in bathtubs, like bathtub gin.
explanation.definitionFit: Absinth is a strong green aniseed-flavoured spirit, an example of an alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: The end is near, capturing Russia in retreat

indicators.note: to capture is to hold inside, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: close means near

indicators.note: retreating means going backwards, so this piece is read in the other direction

parts.note: RU is the international code for Russia

explanation.surface: A war report: the conflict is almost over as an army falls back.
explanation.definitionFit: A closure is a finish or conclusion, as in the closure of a factory, so the end.

clue.text: Fabulous creature to wear piece of cloth inside

indicators.note: the cloth goes inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: to don is to put on clothes, to wear
a rag is a scrap of cloth

explanation.surface: A marvellous animal dresses itself in a scrap of fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fabulous' here means from fable, not wonderful.
explanation.definitionFit: A dragon is a mythical monster from legend and fable, so a fabulous creature in the old sense.

clue.text: Queen's champion backing artificial intelligence

parts.note: a victor is a winner, a champion

indicators.note: backing means moving in the opposite direction, so this piece is read from right to left

parts.note: AI is the common abbreviation

explanation.surface: A royal endorses the technology of machine learning as its champion.
explanation.definitionFit: Victoria was the British monarch who reigned from 1837 to 1901, an example of a queen.

clue.text: Low centre of pants to reveal some flesh

parts.note: a low is the sound a cow makes

indicators.note: the centre of a five-letter word is its third, middle letter

parts.note: the middle letter of the word

explanation.surface: Trousers slung low around the middle so that skin shows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low' looks like an adjective about the trousers, but it is the noun for a cow's call. Pants means underwear in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: To moon is to bare your buttocks at someone as a prank, which shows off some flesh.

clue.text: 1,099 probed by us — sound?

indicators.note: to be probed is to have something pushed inside you

parts.note: in Roman numerals M is 1,000 and IC is 99
taken as written

explanation.surface: Asking whether a number, examined by the team, is reliable.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is by example: music is one kind of sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Music is organised sound, so it is an example of sound, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Bring tea baked in tin with vegetable

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Sn is the chemical symbol for tin

indicators.note: baking changes the form of what goes in the oven, so these letters come out rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A cooking instruction: serve tea alongside a tin-baked dish of greens.
explanation.definitionFit: A string bean is a green bean eaten in its pod, a kind of vegetable.

clue.text: Starter's delightful, they say, in part

indicators.note: only part of the word is wanted, so its tail is dropped
what people say is heard rather than read, so the word goes by its pronunciation

parts.note: super means delightful; the sound can be spelt as shown

explanation.surface: A diner praises the first course as lovely, at least partly.
explanation.walkthrough: Super spoken aloud can be written SOUPER; keep the first part of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Soup is a typical first course served before the main meal, so it is an example of a starter.

clue.text: Adult exits station, not about to leave eating posh dessert

indicators.note: about means turned around, so this word is read backwards
something that eats takes another thing inside it
whatever exits leaves the word, so it is taken out
these letters also leave the word, dropping out

parts.note: Paddington is a major London railway station
taken as written
A is the film-rating abbreviation for adult
U means upper-class, posh

explanation.surface: A grown-up leaves a station, not wanting to go while eating a fancy pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: Paddington is a London railway terminus; 'not about' is a reversed word dropped from it, not a negation. U for upper-class is an old British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Pudding is the everyday British word for the sweet course at the end of a meal, a synonym for dessert.

clue.text: Elegant friend of Barbie in yellow

parts.note: chic means stylish, elegant
Ken is the boyfriend doll of Barbie

explanation.surface: A stylish doll companion of Barbie dressed in a yellow outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yellow' reads as a colour of clothes, but it is the slang for cowardly.
explanation.definitionFit: Both chicken and yellow are informal adjectives for cowardly or lacking courage.
